wreak

REEK -- from Old English wrecan, 'to drive out, punish, avenge'; the same root as wreck. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To wreak is to cause damage, havoc, or destruction to something, often in the phrase 'wreak havoc'.

A single overturned truck wreaked havoc on rush-hour traffic across the whole downtown grid.

Worked Example

The escaped goat spent one afternoon in the community garden and somehow managed to trample the tomatoes, knock over three trellises, and eat an entire row of lettuce.

That kind of sudden, widespread damage caused by one loose cause -- one goat, one storm, one glitch -- is exactly what it means to wreak havoc.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unleash: To unleash is to let a powerful pent-up force go all at once -- unleash a flood, unleash a storm of criticism -- and the word points at the sudden moment of release. To wreak is to work the damage itself, fast or slow, once trouble is already loose.

impose: To impose is to force something unwelcome on people from a position of power -- a new fee, a curfew, a stricter rule -- and it is always someone's deliberate decision. Wreak is chaotic: storms, blunders, and breakdowns wreak damage without anyone decreeing it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

repair: to fix or restore something damaged

forestall: to prevent something by acting first

Where it sits · the scale of damage it causes — inflict → wreak → devastate

inflict vs. wreak: Inflict is a broad word for causing any unpleasant thing to happen to someone, from a minor inconvenience to real harm. Wreak is stronger and almost always paired with a word like 'havoc' or 'destruction,' picturing large-scale chaos.

devastate vs. wreak: Devastate is stronger than wreak, and it aims at the victim directly: a hurricane devastates a coastline, leaving wholesale ruin. Wreak takes the damage as its object instead -- a glitch wreaks havoc -- and the harm it names can stop well short of ruin.

The pieces

root — wrek-

Put it together

Put it together: Wreak comes from Old English wrecan, 'to drive out, punish, avenge' -- the same Germanic root behind wreck -- so to wreak damage is, at its root, closely tied to the idea of a punishing, wrecking force.
